title: If and When
overview: This unit is about a plan that depends on something else. You will say what you will do if a thing happens, and what you will do when it goes wrong. You will join two moments with while, until and as soon as, and keep the time part of a sentence in the present. You will also tell apart what is happening now and what is arranged for later.
learningPath: Meet 26 words for faults, conditions, timing and getting ready.
Read a counter dialogue, an information page and a real building notice.
Learn if plus the present, will in the other half: one day, not every day.
Join two moments with while, until and as soon as.
Keep the time part in the present: when the parcel comes, I will ring you.
Tell apart doing it now and doing it on Friday, by the time word.
Give and write a set of instructions for what to do when something stops.
Speak, write, check every answer against the key, then take the quiz and record the assignment.
lectureScript:
Welcome to Unit 18. This unit is about what you will do if something happens.
A plan often depends on something else. If the bus comes, you will be on time. If it does not, you will not.
And sometimes a thing goes wrong, and you have to say what you will do next.
Start with the words.
An emergency is a sudden, dangerous situation that you must deal with at once.
A breakdown is when a machine or a vehicle stops working and will not go.
A fault is the thing wrong inside it. The breakdown is what happens. The fault is why.
Insurance is money you pay regularly, so that you are covered if something goes wrong.
A refund is money given back to you when you return a thing you bought.
A complaint is when you tell somebody that something was wrong, and ask them to put it right.
A replacement is a new thing, given in place of a broken one.
A guarantee is a promise from the maker to repair or replace a thing for a set time.
These are examples of ordinary words. The rules are different in different places, so this unit teaches the language and not what you should do.
Now the words for what a plan depends on.
A condition is something that must be true before another thing can happen.
Unless means if not. Unless it rains, I will walk.
Whether is for a choice between two sides. I do not know whether it is open.
A possibility is a thing that may happen. A requirement is a thing you must have.
Circumstances are the facts around a situation, and they can change.
Then the timing words. Until means up to the moment something happens. Whenever means every time, or at any time. Ahead means in front, or earlier than you need to. Urgent means it cannot wait. Gradually means slowly, a little at a time. Temporarily means for a short time only.
Last, the getting ready words. Pack, store, replace, inspect, secure and backup.
Now the first pattern.
If it rains tomorrow, I will take the bus.
There are two halves. The if half is in the present. The other half takes will.
This is one occasion, not a law. You already know if you heat ice, it melts. That one is true every time, so it needs no will. This one is about tomorrow, and it may not happen at all.
Say it with me. If the shop is shut, I will come back on Monday.
Second pattern. While, until and as soon as.
While means during the same stretch of time. I will read while I wait.
Until means up to the moment, and not after it. I will wait until she calls.
As soon as means the very moment it happens, with no gap. I will ring you as soon as it arrives.
Third pattern, and this is the one to watch.
When the parcel comes, I will ring you.
Comes, not will come. The time part stays in the present, even when you are talking about the future.
One will to a sentence. It never goes in the half with when, if, until, before, after or as soon as.
Fourth pattern. Now, or later.
I am checking the form now. I am collecting it on Friday.
Both sentences have the same shape. The time word decides which is which.
Now, at the moment, right now: it is happening while you speak.
On Friday, at nine, next week: it is arranged, and it has not happened yet.
Then read the three texts, do the six practices, and check every answer against the key.
The quiz has twelve questions, and every one explains itself.
Finish with the assignment: one recording and one written plan.

outcomes.cefrDescriptor: I can say what I will do if something happens tomorrow.

outcomes.outcome: Join two moments in a short written text using while, until and as soon as, with the comma in the right place.
outcomes.evidence: Grammar card 2 practice, seven of eight; Practice 3, six of eight; Writing 3 checked against its five criteria.
outcomes.cefrDescriptor: I can join two moments in writing with while, until and as soon as.

outcomes.outcome: Answer a question about a future plan, keeping the time part in the present simple and using will only once.
outcomes.evidence: Grammar card 3 practice, six of eight; Speaking 3 recording with the wills counted; Practice 4 corrections.
outcomes.cefrDescriptor: I can answer a question about my plans without putting will in the time part.

outcomes.outcome: Tell apart what is happening now and what is arranged for later, and say which time word told you.
outcomes.evidence: Grammar card 4 practice, seven of eight; Practice 5, eight of ten; Speaking 4 recording.
outcomes.cefrDescriptor: I can say whether something is happening now or arranged for later.

words.meaning: A sudden, dangerous situation that you must deal with at once.
words.example: In an emergency, ring the number on the notice.
practice: A burst pipe is an emergency; a dripping tap is not.
The notice says what to do in an emergency.
Is this an emergency, or can it wait until Monday?
She stayed calm during the emergency.
words.tutor: Give me four short situations, one at a time, and I will say whether each one is an emergency or something that can wait.

words.meaning: When a machine or a vehicle stops working and will not go.
words.example: The breakdown made the whole delivery late.
practice: There was a breakdown on the road, so the bus did not come.
After the breakdown, they sent another van.
A breakdown in the morning costs you the whole day.
Was it a breakdown, or did it run out of fuel?
words.tutor: Ask me four questions about a breakdown on a bus route, and check that I answer each one in a full sentence.

words.meaning: Something wrong inside a thing that stops it working properly.
words.example: The fault was in the wire, not in the switch.
practice: They found the fault after ten minutes.
Report the fault before you use the machine again.
Which fault did the repair worker fix?
A small fault today becomes a big one next month.
words.tutor: I will describe three machines that stopped working. Ask me where the fault was in each one.

words.meaning: Money you pay regularly, so that you are covered if something goes wrong.
words.example: The insurance covers the van but not the tools inside it.
practice: She rang the insurance office about the broken window.
Does the insurance cover a flood?
The insurance did not cover the phone, because it was too old.
Keep the insurance papers with the guarantee.
words.tutor: Explain in three short sentences what insurance is for, using only words a beginner would know.

words.meaning: Money given back to you when you return a thing you bought.
words.example: They gave a refund because the machine never worked.
practice: Ask for a refund if the part is missing.
The refund took two weeks to arrive.
Would you like a refund, or a new one?
There is no refund once the box is open.
words.starter: I asked for a refund because …
words.tutor: Play the person at a counter. I will ask for a refund, and you ask me two questions before you answer.

words.meaning: When you tell somebody that something was wrong, and ask them to put it right.
words.example: Her complaint was short and polite.
practice: Write the complaint on one page.
The complaint was about the late delivery, not about the price.
Who reads a complaint in a big office?
After the complaint, they sent a new one.
words.tutor: Help me make one polite complaint about a late delivery, in three sentences, with no rude words.

words.meaning: A new thing given to you in place of one that is broken or lost.
words.example: The replacement arrived the next morning.
practice: They sent a replacement instead of a refund.
Is the replacement the same size?
A replacement part costs less than a new machine.
She is waiting for a replacement key.
words.tutor: Ask me four questions about a replacement part, and tell me which of my answers is not a full sentence.

words.meaning: A promise from the maker to repair or replace a thing for a set time.
words.example: The guarantee lasts two years.
practice: Keep the guarantee with the receipt.
The guarantee ended last month, so the repair is not free.
Does the guarantee cover the battery?
A guarantee is a promise, and promises have dates on them.
words.tutor: Tell me what a guarantee usually promises, and then ask me two questions to see if I understood.

words.meaning: Something that must be true before another thing can happen.
words.example: There is one condition: you must keep the receipt.
practice: The offer has one condition.
What is the condition for a free repair?
They agreed, on the condition that the work finished on Friday.
Read the conditions before you sign.
words.tutor: Give me three offers, each with one condition, and I will say the condition back to you.

words.meaning: If not. Unless it rains means the same as if it does not rain.
words.example: Unless it rains, I will walk.
practice: I will come unless the bus is late.
Unless you keep the slip, they will not help.
They will not send a replacement unless you report the fault.
Unless it is urgent, wait until Monday.
words.tutor: Say four sentences to me with if not, and I will say each one again using unless.

words.meaning: A word for a choice between two sides, used after know, ask, say and depend.
words.example: I do not know whether it is open.
practice: Ask whether they have a replacement.
She could not say whether the fault was ours.
Tell me whether you want a refund.
It depends on whether the part arrives today.
words.tutor: Ask me four questions that start with Do you know whether, and check that my answers are full sentences.

words.meaning: A thing that may happen, but is not certain.
words.example: There is a possibility of rain tomorrow.
practice: A breakdown is always a possibility on a long trip.
Is there any possibility of a refund?
They talked about every possibility before they decided.
The possibility is small, but it is real.
words.tutor: Give me three possibilities for tomorrow, and I will answer with what I will do in each case.

words.meaning: A thing you must have, or must do, before something can happen.
words.example: A signature is a requirement on this form.
practice: The first requirement is your name.
What are the requirements for an urgent repair?
A receipt is not a requirement here.
They added one more requirement last week.
words.tutor: List three requirements for filling in a form, and then ask me to repeat them back to you.

words.meaning: The facts around a situation, which can change what happens.
words.example: In these circumstances, they made an exception.
practice: The circumstances were different last year.
Under normal circumstances the repair takes a day.
What circumstances would change your plan?
She explained the circumstances in two sentences.
words.tutor: Describe two different circumstances for a late delivery, and ask me what I would do in each one.

words.meaning: Up to the moment when something happens, and not after it.
words.example: I will wait until she calls.
practice: The lift is out of order until Monday.
Do not open the box until you have read the card.
She stayed until the repair worker arrived.
Until the part comes, the machine cannot run.
words.tutor: Say four sentences with until, and tell me if I ever put will in the wrong half.

words.meaning: Every time, or at any time that suits you.
words.example: Whenever the machine stops, report it.
practice: Ring the desk whenever you need help.
Whenever it rains, that road floods.
Come whenever you are ready.
Whenever I pack ahead, the morning is easier.
words.tutor: Ask me four questions starting with Whenever, and check that my answers stay in the present.

words.meaning: In front of you, or earlier than you need to.
words.example: Pack the bag ahead, the night before.
practice: Plan the week ahead on a Sunday.
The road ahead is closed.
If you book ahead, you will get a seat.
She finished the work two days ahead.
words.starter: I will get ready ahead by …
words.tutor: Give me three things that are easier if you do them ahead, and then ask me for one more.

words.meaning: So important that it cannot wait.
words.example: Mark the card urgent only if it cannot wait.
practice: This repair is urgent, because water is coming in.
Is the message urgent, or can I read it later?
An urgent job goes to the top of the list.
Nothing on the desk is urgent this morning.
words.tutor: I will name four jobs. Tell me which are urgent and why, in one sentence each.

words.meaning: Slowly, a little at a time.
words.example: The battery gradually stopped holding its charge.
practice: The noise got worse gradually, over several weeks.
Add the water gradually, not all at once.
She gradually learned the whole route.
Did it break suddenly, or gradually?
words.tutor: Give me three things that change gradually and three that change suddenly, then ask me to sort them.

words.meaning: For a short time only, not for good.
words.example: The lift is temporarily out of order.
practice: They temporarily closed the road.
I am temporarily using the old machine.
The desk is temporarily on the second floor.
The notice says the shop is temporarily shut.
words.tutor: Say four sentences with temporarily, and check that I put the word in the right place each time.

words.meaning: Put things into a bag or a box, ready to carry or to send.
words.example: I will pack the bag tonight.
practice: Pack the tools before you lock the van.
She packed the box and wrote the address on it.
If you pack ahead, the morning is easier.
What did you pack for the trip?
words.tutor: Ask me what I will pack for a short trip, and then ask two more questions about it.

words.meaning: Keep something in a safe place until you need it.
words.example: Store the papers in one folder.
practice: We store the spare parts in the back room.
Store the guarantee with the receipt.
Where do you store the winter clothes?
They stored the boxes until the shop opened.
words.tutor: Tell me three places people store important papers, and ask me where I store mine. I may invent it.

words.meaning: Put a new thing in the place of an old or broken one.
words.example: Replace the battery before it fails.
practice: They will replace the part on Friday.
If you replace it early, the machine will not stop.
Who replaced the broken window?
I need to replace this bag.
words.tutor: Give me four sentences with replace, and tell me which one is about a thing and which is about a person.

words.meaning: Look at something carefully to see whether it is right.
words.example: A repair worker will inspect the fault.
practice: Inspect the wire before you use the heater.
She inspected every box in the van.
Who will inspect the work when it is finished?
If you inspect it now, you will find the split.
words.tutor: Tell me three things worth inspecting before a long trip, and then ask me to add one.

words.meaning: Fix or fasten something so that it cannot move, fall or be taken.
words.example: Secure the lid before you lift the box.
practice: Secure the ladder before you climb it.
They secured the load with two straps.
Is the door secured for the night?
If you secure the boxes, nothing will move.
words.tutor: Name three things you can secure in a van, and ask me how I would secure each one.

words.meaning: A second copy, or a second plan, kept in case the first one fails.
words.example: Keep a backup of every important paper.
practice: The backup was on an old phone.
Make a backup before you clear the folder.
What is your backup if the bus does not come?
A backup costs nothing until you need it.
words.tutor: Ask me what my backup plan is for getting to a morning appointment, and then ask me why.

grammar.title: If it rains tomorrow, I will take the bus
grammar.explanation: Some plans depend on something else. If the first thing happens, the second one follows. The if half stays in the present simple. The other half takes will. This is one future occasion, and it may not happen at all.
grammar.rule:
If plus the present simple, then will plus the verb.
If it rains tomorrow, I will take the bus.
If the shop is shut, I will come back on Monday.
If the parcel arrives today, I will ring you.
Turn it round and the comma goes:
I will take the bus if it rains tomorrow.
Negative in the if half:
If the lift is not working, I will use the stairs.
Unless means if not:
Unless it rains, I will walk.
Question:
What will you do if the train is late?
Never put will in the if half. Not: If it will rain.
grammar.workedExample:
One done, step by step.
You want to say this: maybe the bus does not come, and then you walk.
Two halves. Ask which one depends on the other.
The walking depends on the bus, so the bus half takes if.
Put the if half in the present simple: If the bus does not come.
Put will in the other half: I will walk.
Join them. The if half comes first, so add a comma.
Answer: If the bus does not come, I will walk.
Now turn it round: I will walk if the bus does not come. No comma this time.
grammar.mistake: It is easy to write if it will rain, I will take the bus. English keeps will out of the if half: If it rains, I will take the bus. The other slip is using this pattern for a fact. You already know if you heat ice, it melts. Ice melts every time, so that one takes no will at all. This card is about one day only.
grammar.tip: One will to a sentence, and never in the half with if.
grammar.practice:
Make one sentence from each pair. Put if in front of the first half, and will in the second half. Add a comma after the if half.
1. it rains tomorrow / I take the bus
2. the shop is shut / I come back on Monday
3. the parcel arrives today / I ring you
4. they do not send a replacement / I ask for a refund
5. you report the fault / they inspect the wire
6. the guarantee ends / the repair cost me money
7. I pack the bag tonight / I am ready by six
8. the machine breaks down again / we use the old one
grammar.answers:
1. If it rains tomorrow, I will take the bus.
2. If the shop is shut, I will come back on Monday.
3. If the parcel arrives today, I will ring you.
4. If they do not send a replacement, I will ask for a refund.
5. If you report the fault, they will inspect the wire.
6. If the guarantee ends, the repair will cost me money.
7. If I pack the bag tonight, I will be ready by six.
8. If the machine breaks down again, we will use the old one.
The likeliest wrong answer is 1: writing if it will rain tomorrow. Will belongs in the other half only.
Item 7 catches people too. I am ready becomes I will be ready, because the whole sentence is about tomorrow.

grammar.title: Until she calls, as soon as it arrives, while I wait
grammar.explanation: Three words join two things in time. While means during the same stretch of time. Until means up to the moment something happens, and not after it. As soon as means the very moment it happens, with no gap at all.
grammar.rule:
while: at the same time as
I will read while I wait.
While the machine is being inspected, I will use the old one.
until: up to that moment, and no further
I will wait until she calls.
The lift is out of order until Monday.
as soon as: the moment it happens, with no gap
I will ring you as soon as it arrives.
As soon as the fault is fixed, I will collect the kettle.
Each one can start the sentence or sit in the middle.
At the front, put a comma after its half:
Until she calls, I will wait.
In the middle, use no comma:
I will wait until she calls.
grammar.workedExample:
One done, step by step.
You want to say: you are in the waiting room, and you read the whole time.
Ask: is this a stretch of time, a stopping point, or one moment?
The reading fills a stretch, so the word is while.
Build it: I will read while I wait.
Now change the meaning. You read, and you stop the moment your name is called.
That is a stopping point, so the word is until: I will read until they call my name.
Now change it again. The moment your name is called, you stand up.
That is one moment with no gap, so it is as soon as: As soon as they call my name, I will stand up.
One comma, because the time half comes first.
grammar.mistake: It is easy to write I will wait until she will call. Until takes the present, even about the future: I will wait until she calls. The other slip is using while for a single moment, as in while the parcel arrives. While needs a stretch of time, so write as soon as the parcel arrives.
grammar.tip: While is a stretch. Until is a line you stop at. As soon as is a door opening.
grammar.practice:
Choose while, until or as soon as.
1. I will read the notice ____ I wait at the desk.
2. Do not open the box ____ you have read the card.
3. ____ the part arrives, they will fit it the same morning.
4. The road is closed ____ Friday.
5. ____ the van was being repaired, we used a taxi.
6. Ring me ____ you hear from them, even if it is late.
7. She stayed at the counter ____ the repair worker came.
8. ____ I pack the bag, you can inspect the wire.
grammar.answers:
1. while 2. until 3. As soon as 4. until 5. While 6. as soon as 7. until 8. While
The likeliest wrong answer is 3: choosing while. Fitting a part is one moment, not a stretch, so as soon as is the one.
Item 6 catches people too. As soon as carries the meaning without delay, which until cannot.
Eight of eight: move on. Six or seven: read the rule again and redo the two you missed. Five or fewer: read the card from the top and do it once more.

grammar.title: When the parcel comes, I will ring you: no will in the time part
grammar.explanation: A sentence about the future often has two parts: when a thing happens, and what you will do. Only one part takes will. The time part stays in the present simple, even though it has not happened yet.
grammar.rule:
Time words that work this way: when, before, after, until, as soon as, whenever, once.
When the parcel comes, I will ring you.
After I finish work, I will inspect the wire.
Before you pack the bag, I will check the list.
As soon as the guarantee ends, I will replace it.
Whenever the machine stops, I will report the fault.
The if half from the first card behaves the same way.
Not: when the parcel will come.
Put the time part first and add a comma.
Put it second and drop the comma:
I will ring you when the parcel comes.
grammar.workedExample:
One done, step by step.
You want to say: the part arrives, and then you fit it.
Two parts. Which one is the time part?
The part arriving is the time part, because it says when.
The time part keeps the present simple: when the part arrives.
The other part takes will: I will fit it.
Count the wills. One, and it is not in the time part. Good.
Time part first, so add a comma.
Answer: When the part arrives, I will fit it.
Second version, no comma: I will fit it when the part arrives.
grammar.mistake: It is easy to write I will ring you when the parcel will come. That is two wills in one sentence. English keeps the time part in the present: when the parcel comes. Say the sentence out loud and count the wills. One is right, two is not.
grammar.tip: Count the wills. One to a sentence, and never after when, until, after, before or as soon as.
grammar.practice:
One verb in each pair is wrong. Write the whole sentence correctly.
1. When the parcel will come, I will ring you.
2. I will inspect the wire after I will finish work.
3. As soon as the guarantee will end, I will replace the machine.
4. Whenever the machine will stop, I will report the fault.
5. Before you will pack the bag, I will check the list.
6. I will wait at the desk until they will call my name.
7. Once the road will open, the delivery will come.
8. When the circumstances will change, we will make a new plan.
grammar.answers:
1. When the parcel comes, I will ring you.
2. I will inspect the wire after I finish work.
3. As soon as the guarantee ends, I will replace the machine.
4. Whenever the machine stops, I will report the fault.
5. Before you pack the bag, I will check the list.
6. I will wait at the desk until they call my name.
7. Once the road opens, the delivery will come.
8. When the circumstances change, we will make a new plan.
The likeliest wrong answer is 7: taking the will out of both halves. One half still needs it, and here it is the delivery half.
Item 4 catches people too. Whenever takes the present simple just like when does.

grammar.title: Doing it now, or doing it on Friday: the time word decides
grammar.explanation: Am, is or are plus an -ing verb does two jobs. With now it is happening while you speak. With a day or a clock time it is arranged and has not happened yet. The verb looks the same, so the time word is what tells you which.
grammar.rule:
Happening now:
I am checking the form now.
She is inspecting the wire at the moment.
They are packing the van right now.
Arranged for later:
I am collecting it on Friday.
She is inspecting the wire at nine tomorrow.
They are replacing the pump next week.
Now, at the moment, right now: it is happening.
On Friday, at nine, tomorrow, next week: it is arranged.
Arranged means fixed. Somebody has agreed it, or it is written down.
A guess takes will instead: I think it will rain.
A decision you have only just made takes going to: I am going to ring them.
grammar.workedExample:
One done, step by step.
The sentence is: I am collecting the replacement on Friday.
First find the time word. It is on Friday.
Ask: is that now, or later? Friday is later.
So the sentence is arranged, not happening.
Mark it L for later.
Now take the time word away: I am collecting the replacement.
Without it, nobody can tell whether the box is in your hands or still in the shop.
Put a different time word in: I am collecting the replacement right now.
Same verb, new meaning. Mark that one N for now.
grammar.mistake: It is easy to write I am collecting it and leave the time word out. Then a reader cannot tell whether the box is in your hands or still in the shop. Add the time word: I am collecting it on Friday.
grammar.tip: Look for the time word first. Now means now. A day or a clock time means later.
grammar.practice:
Write N if it is happening now, or L if it is arranged for later. Then write the time word that told you.
1. I am packing the bag right now.
2. She is inspecting the van at nine tomorrow.
3. They are replacing the pump next week.
4. He is filling in the complaint form at the moment.
5. We are storing the boxes in the back room this afternoon.
6. The repair worker is coming on Thursday.
7. I am waiting at the counter now.
8. They are closing the road temporarily next month.
grammar.answers:
1. N, right now 2. L, at nine tomorrow 3. L, next week 4. N, at the moment 5. L, this afternoon 6. L, on Thursday 7. N, now 8. L, next month
The likeliest wrong answer is 5: marking it N. This afternoon has not arrived yet, so the boxes are still to be moved.
Seven or eight right: move on. Five or six: read the rule column again. Four or fewer: do the worked example again, then this practice.

readings.title: At the counter
readings.setting: A shop counter, three weeks after a kettle was bought
readings.passage:
You: Good morning. I bought this kettle here three weeks ago. It has stopped working.
Shop assistant: I am sorry. Let me look. Do you have the receipt?
You: Yes. Here it is.
Shop assistant: Thank you. It is still inside the guarantee, so we can help. Would you like a replacement or a refund?
You: What is the difference?
Shop assistant: If you take a replacement, I will give you a new kettle today. If you want a refund, I will send this one away first. Somebody will inspect it. That takes about two weeks.
You: Why does it take so long?
Shop assistant: They have to find the fault. If the fault is ours, you will get the money back. If it is not, they will send the kettle back to you.
You: I will take the replacement, then.
Shop assistant: A good choice. I will fetch one from the store room. Wait here until I come back.
You: Is there a form?
Shop assistant: One line. Write today's date and sign it. As soon as you sign, the old guarantee moves across to the new kettle.
You: And if the new one stops too?
Shop assistant: Then come back and bring this slip. Unless the kettle is damaged, we will replace it again.
You: Thank you.
Shop assistant: Here you are. I will pack it for you. If you store the slip somewhere safe, you will not need the old receipt again.

This is a made-up shop. The rules are not the same everywhere.

readings.title: Ready before it goes wrong
readings.setting: A page from a booklet about looking after your own things
readings.passage:
Things break. A machine stops, a wire comes loose, a bag splits. You cannot stop that. What you can do is get ready ahead of the day it happens, so that a breakdown costs you an afternoon and not a week.

Inspect. Look at a thing before you need it. If you inspect the bag now, you will find the split while there is still time to mend it. A fault found early is a small fault.

Secure. Fasten the loose things. A box that is not secure moves, and a thing that moves gets damaged. Tie it, clip it, shut the lid.

Pack ahead. If you pack the night before, you will not stand in the hall at six in the morning looking for one glove. Put the bag by the door.

Store what you keep. Keep the papers for a thing in one place: the receipt, the guarantee, the insurance, and any complaint you have made. Whenever you need one, you will know where it is.

Replace before it fails. Some things wear out gradually. A brush, a battery, a pair of shoes. If you replace the battery while it still works, the machine will not stop on the morning you need it most.

Make a backup. A backup is a second copy, or a second plan. If you keep a photograph of an important paper, you will still have the information when the paper is lost.

None of this makes an emergency impossible. It makes an emergency smaller. When something goes wrong, the useful question is not whose fault it is. The useful question is what you will do next, and whether you are ready to do it.

readings.title: Building notice and repair card
readings.setting: A notice board beside the front desk of a building
readings.passage:
BUILDING NOTICE AND REPAIR CARD

LIFT OUT OF ORDER
The lift is temporarily out of order. A fault was reported on Tuesday morning.
Use the stairs until further notice.
If you cannot use the stairs, ring the desk on 20 84 22 and somebody will come to you.

HOW TO REPORT A FAULT
1. Write down what happened, and when.
2. Fill in a repair card at the desk. One card, one fault.
3. Mark the card urgent only if it is an emergency: water, smoke, or a person shut in.
4. Give the card to the person at the desk. Do not leave it on the counter.
5. Keep the yellow half of the card. It carries the number you will need.

WHAT HAPPENS NEXT
As soon as the card reaches the office, a repair worker will inspect the fault.
If the repair is quick, they will do it the same day.
If a part is needed, they will order it. That takes up to five working days.
You will be told which of the two it is before the end of the day.

CONDITIONS
A repair card is not a complaint. If you want to make a complaint, use a white form.
The building insurance does not cover a thing you brought in yourself.
There is no refund and no replacement for a personal item.

REQUIREMENTS FOR AN URGENT CARD
Your name and the floor number.
The time you found the fault.
One line saying why it cannot wait until tomorrow.

Unless the desk is shut, a card is read on the day it is handed in. In other circumstances it is read the next morning.

This is an example notice. The wording is different in every building.

comprehension.q: What does the shop assistant ask for before offering any help?
comprehension.why: The second line is: Do you have the receipt? Everything after it depends on the answer being yes.

comprehension.q: Which is faster, the replacement or the refund, and by how long?
comprehension.a: The replacement. It is given the same day, and the refund takes about two weeks.
comprehension.why: The assistant offers a new kettle today. The refund route takes about two weeks, because the kettle must first be sent away and inspected.

comprehension.q: The assistant says, unless the kettle is damaged, we will replace it again. What would stop the shop replacing it?
comprehension.a: Damage. If the kettle is damaged, the shop will not replace it a second time.
comprehension.why: Unless means if not, so the promise holds in every case except one: the kettle being damaged. That is the one condition the assistant names.

comprehension.q: What does the text say a backup is?
comprehension.a: A second copy, or a second plan.
comprehension.why: The backup paragraph defines it in its first line, and then gives the example of a photograph of an important paper.

comprehension.q: The text says some things wear out gradually. What does gradually tell you about how they break?
comprehension.a: That they get worse slowly, a little at a time, rather than stopping all at once.
comprehension.why: The examples given are a brush, a battery and a pair of shoes. None of them fails in one moment, which is why the text says to replace them while they still work.

comprehension.q: Why does the text say the useful question is not whose fault it is?
comprehension.a: Because asking whose fault it is changes nothing, while asking what you will do next gets the problem solved.
comprehension.why: The whole page is about being ready before the day something breaks. The last paragraph says an emergency cannot be made impossible, only smaller, so the writer points the reader at the next step instead of at blame.

comprehension.type: What a person would do next
comprehension.q: You find water coming through a ceiling on the second floor. What do you fill in, how do you mark it, and what three things must you write?
comprehension.a: Fill in a repair card at the desk and mark it urgent. Write your name and the floor number, the time you found the fault, and one line saying why it cannot wait until tomorrow.
comprehension.why: Water is one of the three things the notice names as an emergency, so the urgent mark is allowed. The requirements list then gives exactly three things an urgent card must carry.

comprehension.q: Your own radio breaks while it is in the building. Will the building give you a replacement?
comprehension.a: No. The notice says there is no refund and no replacement for a personal item.
comprehension.why: The conditions section says the building insurance does not cover a thing you brought in yourself. It then rules out both a refund and a replacement for a personal item.

comprehension.q: You hand a card in at four in the afternoon and the desk is open. When will it be read?
comprehension.why: The last line says that unless the desk is shut, a card is read on the day it is handed in. The desk is open, so the exception does not apply.

speaking.title: Speaking 1 — If it happens, I will
speaking.instructions:
Say these eight lines out loud. Then record them and play them back.
If it rains tomorrow, I will take the bus.
If the shop is shut, I will come back on Monday.
If the parcel arrives today, I will ring you.
If they do not send a replacement, I will ask for a refund.
If the lift is out of order, I will use the stairs.
Unless it is urgent, I will wait until Monday.
I will pack the bag tonight if I finish work early.
What will you do if the train is late?
Now make eight of your own about the week ahead. You may invent every detail.
Play your recording back.
Check one thing only: count the wills in each sentence.
One will is right. Two is not, and the extra one is always in the if half.
speaking.tutor: Give me six half sentences that start with if, and I will finish each one with will. Tell me if I ever put will in the if half.

speaking.title: Speaking 2 — While, until, as soon as
speaking.instructions:
Say each pair out loud, then record the whole set and play it back.
I will read while I wait.
I will read until they call my name.
I will stand up as soon as they call my name.
She is at the desk while the van is being repaired.
She is at the desk until the van comes back.
She will leave as soon as the van comes back.
Now say three of your own for each word, about an ordinary day.
Play the recording back and ask one question of every sentence.
Is this a stretch of time, a stopping point, or one single moment?
A stretch takes while. A stopping point takes until. One moment takes as soon as.
Say again any sentence where the answer and the word do not match.
speaking.tutor: Describe three short situations to me. For each one ask whether I would use while, until or as soon as, and tell me if my reason is wrong.

speaking.title: Speaking 3 — Answering a question about your plans
speaking.instructions:
These six questions are asked of you. Answer each one out loud in a full sentence. Record your answers.
What will you do when you finish this unit?
Where will you go after you leave the house tomorrow?
Who will you ring as soon as you get the news?
What will you do if the bus does not come?
How long will you wait until you ask somebody?
What will you do whenever the machine stops?
Every answer has two parts: a time part and a will part.
Play the recording back and count the wills in each answer.
One will, and never in the time part. Say any answer again that has two.
You may invent any detail in your answers.
speaking.tutor: Ask me the six questions from Speaking 3, one at a time, and after each answer tell me how many wills I used and where.

speaking.title: Speaking 4 — Now, or on Friday
speaking.instructions:
Say these six pairs out loud and record them.
I am checking the form now. I am checking the form at nine tomorrow.
She is inspecting the wire at the moment. She is inspecting the wire on Thursday.
They are packing the van right now. They are packing the van next week.
Now say six pairs of your own, about work or about where you study.
Play the recording back.
After each sentence say one word out loud: now, or later.
If you cannot decide, the time word is missing. Say that sentence again with a time word in it.
speaking.tutor: Say eight sentences to me with am, is or are plus an -ing verb, some about now and some arranged. I will say now or later for each, and you tell me which time word decided it.

speaking.title: Speaking 5 — Tell somebody what to do when it stops
speaking.instructions:
A machine you use has stopped working. Say out loud, in order, what a person should do. You may invent the machine.
Give five steps. Start each one with the verb.
Join the steps with these words: first, then, after that, as soon as, until, finally.
A model, said aloud:
First, switch it off at the wall.
Then inspect the wire and the plug for a fault.
After that, write down what happened and when.
As soon as the desk is open, report the fault.
Finally, wait until they ring you, and keep the slip.
Record your five steps and play them back.
Check three things you can count: five steps, five different joining words, and a verb at the start of every step.
If a step is missing a verb at the front, say that step again.
speaking.tutor: Listen to my five steps for a machine that has stopped, then say them back to me in order and tell me if any two steps could be swapped without breaking the sequence.

speaking.title: Speaking 6 — My plan, and my backup
speaking.instructions:
Speak for one minute about tomorrow. You may invent every detail.
Say one thing that is arranged: use am, is or are plus -ing with a time word.
Say one thing that depends on something else: use if plus the present and will.
Say what you will do as soon as the first thing is finished.
Say how long you will wait, using until.
Say your backup, using unless or if not.
Record the minute and play it back.
Count five things: one arrangement, one if sentence, one as soon as, one until, one backup.
If one is missing, record the minute again rather than adding it in your head.
speaking.tutor: I will describe my plan for tomorrow in one minute. Tell me which of these five I used: an arrangement, an if sentence, as soon as, until, and a backup.

writing.title: Writing 1 — Four things that depend on something else
writing.prompt: Write four sentences about the week ahead. Each one says what you will do if something happens. You may invent every detail. Use unless in one of the four.
writing.model:
If the parcel arrives on Tuesday, I will ring the office the same afternoon.
If the lift is still out of order, I will use the stairs.
Unless it rains, I will walk to the market on Saturday.
If the shop cannot repair it, I will ask for a replacement.
writing.starter: If the parcel arrives on Tuesday, I will
writing.criteria: Four sentences. Every sentence has an if half in the present simple and a will half. One sentence uses unless. Every if half that comes first is followed by a comma. Each sentence has exactly one will.
writing.support: Do one first, in two steps. Write the if half only: If the parcel arrives on Tuesday. Then add the will half: I will ring the office. Join them with a comma and the sentence is finished.
writing.extension: Add a fifth sentence with the if half at the end instead of the front, and take the comma out.

writing.title: Writing 2 — What to do when it stops
writing.prompt: Write a short set of instructions for a person who has never done this. The machine they use has stopped working. You may invent the machine. Give it a title and five numbered steps.
writing.model:
What to do if the heater stops
1. Switch it off at the wall before you touch anything else.
2. Inspect the wire and the plug. Look for a fault you can see.
3. Write down what happened and the time it happened.
4. Report the fault at the desk as soon as it opens.
5. Keep the slip until the repair is finished.
writing.length: A title and five numbered steps
writing.criteria: A title and five numbered steps. Every step starts with a verb. Every step is one sentence. At least two steps use a time word: before, after, until or as soon as. No step needs another person to be present.
writing.support: Write the five verbs first, in order, and nothing else: switch, inspect, write, report, keep. Then add the rest of each line around its verb.
writing.extension: Add a short line under the list that begins: Do not, and names the one thing a person should never do first.

writing.title: Writing 3 — A message that joins two moments
writing.prompt: Write a message of five sentences to somebody who is waiting for news from you. Say what is happening now, what you are waiting for, and what you will do when it comes. You may invent every detail.
writing.model:
I am waiting at the counter at the moment.
They are inspecting the machine while I wait.
I will stay here until they tell me the price of the repair.
As soon as I know, I will send you a message.
Unless the part is missing, I should be home by six.
writing.starter: I am waiting at the counter
writing.criteria: Five sentences. One uses while, one uses until, and one uses as soon as. Every time word that starts a sentence is followed by a comma. No sentence has will in its time half. Every sentence ends with a full stop.
writing.support: Write the three joining words down the side of the page first: while, until, as soon as. Then write one sentence beside each, and add the other two sentences afterwards.
writing.extension: Add a sixth sentence that says what you will do whenever this happens, not only this time.

writing.title: Writing 4 — Saturday, and what I will do if it goes wrong
writing.prompt: Write two short paragraphs about next Saturday. You may invent every detail. Paragraph one: what is arranged, and at what time. Paragraph two: two things that could go wrong, and what you will do in each case.
writing.model:
I am collecting a replacement on Saturday morning. The shop is opening at nine, and I am meeting a neighbour outside at ten past. After that we are going to the market. I am packing the bag on Friday night, so the morning is easier.

Two things could go wrong. If the shop has no replacement, I will ask for a refund instead. If the bus does not come, I will walk, and I will ring the neighbour as soon as I leave the house. Unless it rains hard, the walk takes half an hour.
writing.starter: I am collecting a replacement on
writing.length: Two paragraphs, four to five sentences each
writing.criteria: Two paragraphs. Paragraph one has at least two arranged sentences, each with a time word. Paragraph two has at least two if sentences, each with one will. One sentence uses unless or as soon as. Every paragraph starts with a capital letter and every sentence ends with a full stop.
writing.support: Make two lists before you write. List one: three things and the time of each. List two: two things that could go wrong. Then turn each line of list one into an -ing sentence, and each line of list two into an if sentence.
writing.extension: Add one line at the end that names your backup, starting: If both of those happen,

activities.title: Practice 1 — Which word?
activities.instructions:
Write one word in each gap.
Use: emergency, breakdown, fault, insurance, refund, complaint, replacement, guarantee.
1. Money given back to you when you return a thing is a ____ .
2. A promise from the maker to repair a thing for a set time is a ____ .
3. A new thing given in place of a broken one is a ____ .
4. Water coming through a ceiling is an ____ .
5. The thing wrong inside the machine is the ____ .
6. Money you pay regularly, so that you are covered, is ____ .
7. When a van stops on the road and will not go, that is a ____ .
8. When you tell a shop that something was wrong, that is a ____ .
activities.answers:
1. refund 2. guarantee 3. replacement 4. emergency 5. fault 6. insurance 7. breakdown 8. complaint
Eight of eight: move on. Six or seven: read the word cards for the ones you missed. Five or fewer: read all eight cards again, then do this once more.
activities.solo: Cover the word list with your hand for the first four items. Uncover it only if you are stuck, and mark which ones needed it.

activities.title: Practice 2 — Match the word to the meaning
activities.instructions:
Match each word to its meaning. Write the number and the letter.
Words: 1 condition, 2 whether, 3 possibility, 4 requirement, 5 circumstances, 6 urgent, 7 gradually, 8 temporarily, 9 ahead, 10 backup.
Meanings:
a. For a short time only.
b. A thing you must have before something can happen.
c. Slowly, a little at a time.
d. A second copy, or a second plan.
e. Something that must be true before another thing can happen.
f. The facts around a situation, which can change.
g. So important that it cannot wait.
h. A thing that may happen, but is not certain.
i. A word for a choice between two sides.
j. Earlier than you need to.
activities.answers:
1e 2i 3h 4b 5f 6g 7c 8a 9j 10d
Nine or ten right: move on. Seven or eight: read the two word cards you missed and try those two again. Six or fewer: read the whole It depends group and the Timing group again.
The pair people swap is 1 and 4. A condition is something that must be TRUE; a requirement is something you must HAVE or DO.
activities.solo: Do it twice. The first time, cover the meanings and say each word's meaning out loud from memory. The second time, match them on the page and see how close you were.

activities.title: Practice 3 — While, until or as soon as
activities.instructions:
Write while, until or as soon as in each gap.
1. Do not lift the box ____ you have secured the lid.
2. ____ the desk opens, I will hand the card in.
3. I read the notice ____ I waited for my name.
4. The lift is out of order ____ Friday.
5. ____ the machine was being inspected, we used the old one.
6. Ring me ____ you hear from them, at any hour.
7. She stayed at the counter ____ the repair worker arrived.
8. ____ you pack the bag, I will inspect the wire.
activities.answers:
1. until 2. As soon as 3. while 4. until 5. While 6. as soon as 7. until 8. While
The item people get wrong is 6. As soon as carries the meaning without delay; until would mean the opposite, that you stop ringing at that point.
Seven or eight right: move on. Five or six: read grammar card 2 again. Four or fewer: do the worked example on card 2, then this practice again.
activities.solo: Read each finished sentence out loud before you check the key. If a sentence sounds like two things happening at one instant, the answer is as soon as.

activities.title: Practice 4 — Find the extra will
activities.instructions:
Each sentence has one will too many, or one missing. Write the sentence correctly.
1. If it will rain tomorrow, I will take the bus.
2. I will ring you when the parcel will come.
3. As soon as the part arrives, they fit it.
4. Unless the desk will be shut, I will hand the card in today.
5. I will wait at the counter until they will call my name.
6. Whenever the machine stops, I report the fault to the desk.
7. If the guarantee will end, the repair will cost money.
8. Before you pack the bag, I will inspected the wire.
activities.answers:
1. If it rains tomorrow, I will take the bus.
2. I will ring you when the parcel comes.
3. As soon as the part arrives, they will fit it.
4. Unless the desk is shut, I will hand the card in today.
5. I will wait at the counter until they call my name.
6. Whenever the machine stops, I will report the fault to the desk.
7. If the guarantee ends, the repair will cost money.
8. Before you pack the bag, I will inspect the wire.
Items 3 and 6 are the ones people leave alone. There the will is MISSING from the other half, not extra in the time half.
Item 8 is a different slip: will is always followed by the plain verb, so inspected becomes inspect.
Seven or eight right: move on. Five or six: read grammar cards 1 and 3 again.
activities.solo: Put your finger on each sentence and count the wills out loud before you change anything. One will, outside the time half, is the target.

activities.title: Practice 5 — Now or later
activities.instructions:
Write N for happening now, or L for arranged for later. Then copy the time word that told you.
1. I am packing the bag right now.
2. She is inspecting the van at nine tomorrow.
3. They are replacing the pump next week.
4. He is filling in the complaint form at the moment.
5. We are storing the boxes this afternoon.
6. The repair worker is coming on Thursday.
7. I am waiting at the counter now.
8. They are closing the road temporarily next month.
9. She is reading the guarantee at the moment.
10. I am collecting the replacement on Saturday morning.
activities.answers:
1. N, right now 2. L, at nine tomorrow 3. L, next week 4. N, at the moment 5. L, this afternoon 6. L, on Thursday 7. N, now 8. L, next month 9. N, at the moment 10. L, on Saturday morning
The one people get wrong is 5. This afternoon has not arrived yet, so the boxes have not been moved.
Nine or ten right: move on. Seven or eight: read grammar card 4 again. Six or fewer: do the worked example on card 4 first.
activities.solo: Cover the second column and write only N or L first. Then go back and add the time word. If you cannot find a time word for a line, you have chosen by guessing.

activities.title: Practice 6 — Put the steps in order
activities.instructions:
These five steps are for reporting a fault in a building. They are in the wrong order. Write them as a numbered list, 1 to 5.
a. Keep the yellow half of the card, because it carries the number you will need.
b. Write down what happened and when it happened.
c. Give the card to the person at the desk.
d. Mark the card urgent only if it is an emergency.
e. Fill in a repair card at the desk, one card for one fault.
Then answer two questions in one sentence each.
6. Which step could you do before you reach the building?
7. Which step happens last, and why must it be last?
activities.answers:
1. b 2. e 3. d 4. c 5. a
6. Step b. You can write down what happened and when, wherever you are standing.
7. Step a, keeping the yellow half. The card is not split until it has been handed in, so nothing can be kept before that.
All five in order: move on. Four in order: check Reading 3 and find the one you moved. Three or fewer: read Reading 3 again and copy its list out by hand.
activities.solo: Cover the notice first and try the order from memory. Then uncover Reading 3 and mark how many you had right before you looked.

quizzes.q: Which sentence is about one future day, and not about something that is always true?
options: If it rains tomorrow, I will take the bus.
If you heat ice, it melts.
If you press this button, the light comes on.
If you drop a glass, it breaks.
quizzes.a: If it rains tomorrow, I will take the bus.
quizzes.why: Will points at one moment, and tomorrow names it. The other three are true every time, which is why they take no will at all. The ice one is the tempting choice, because it also starts with if; the test is whether you could say every time in front of it.

quizzes.q: Complete the sentence: If the shop ____ shut, I will come back on Monday.
quizzes.why: The if half stays in the present simple. Will be is the commonest wrong answer, because the sentence is about the future, but English keeps will out of the if half. Was puts the sentence in the past, and is being describes something happening at this second.

options: Unless it does not rain, I will walk.
Unless will it rain, I will walk.
Unless it rains, I will walk.
quizzes.a: Unless it rains, I will walk.
quizzes.why: Unless already means if not, so the meaning is: if it does not rain, I will walk. The first option says not twice and turns the meaning round. The second puts will in the unless half. The last one answers with a past verb for a future plan.

quizzes.q: Choose the word: I will wait ____ she calls.
quizzes.why: The waiting stops at the moment she calls, and until marks that stopping point. While would mean you wait during her call. As soon as would mean you start waiting the moment she calls, which is the opposite. Whenever would make it every time she calls.

quizzes.q: Which sentence means: at the very moment it arrives, with no gap?
options: I will ring you while it arrives.
I will ring you as soon as it arrives.
I will ring you until it arrives.
I will ring you whenever it arrives.
quizzes.a: I will ring you as soon as it arrives.
quizzes.why: As soon as is the one that means with no delay. While needs a stretch of time, and arriving is one moment. Until would mean you stop ringing then. Whenever makes it every time, which cannot be right for one parcel.

options: When the parcel will come, I will ring you.
When the parcel comes, I ring you will.
When the parcel comes, I will ring you.
When the parcel will come, I ring you.
quizzes.a: When the parcel comes, I will ring you.
quizzes.why: The time part keeps the present simple, and the other part takes will. The first option puts will in both halves. The second breaks the word order. The last one has will in the time half only, which is the wrong half.

quizzes.q: Choose the correct pair: I ____ the wire after I ____ work.
quizzes.why: One will to a sentence, and it never goes after the word after. Will inspect and will finish is the tempting answer, because both actions are in the future; only one half may carry will. Inspect and finish drops the will altogether, and will finished puts a past form after will.

quizzes.q: I am collecting it on Friday. What does this sentence tell you?
options: It is arranged, and it has not happened yet.
It is happening while you speak.
It is only a guess about Friday.
quizzes.a: It is arranged, and it has not happened yet.
quizzes.why: On Friday is a day, and a day means later, so the -ing form is an arrangement. It would only mean happening now with a word like now or at the moment. A guess would take will, and every Friday would take the present simple: I collect it on Fridays.

quizzes.q: Which time word shows that the action is happening while you speak?
quizzes.why: At the moment means this second, so the -ing form is happening now. On Friday, next week and tomorrow all point past this second, so with an -ing verb they mean an arrangement instead.

options: the money given back when you return a thing.
a promise to repair a thing for a set time.
a new thing given in place of a broken one.
something wrong inside a thing that stops it working.
quizzes.a: something wrong inside a thing that stops it working.
quizzes.why: A fault is the reason a machine stops. The first option is a refund, the second is a guarantee and the third is a replacement. The word people confuse it with is breakdown: the breakdown is what happens, and the fault is why it happened.

quizzes.q: The notice says the lift is temporarily out of order. What does temporarily mean?
quizzes.why: Temporarily means not for good. For good is its opposite, and the notice would not tell people to use the stairs until further notice if the lift were never coming back. Every morning would be regularly, and at any time you like is whenever.

quizzes.q: Which word means every time, or at any time?
quizzes.why: Whenever covers both every time and at any time that suits you. Ahead means earlier than you need to, unless means if not, and gradually means slowly, a little at a time.

teacherNotes.note: The extra will is the error that lasts longest, and explaining the rule again rarely fixes it, because the learner already agrees with the rule. What fixes it is a counting habit: read the sentence out loud and count the wills on your fingers. One will, and never in the half that begins with if, when, until, before, after or as soon as. Practice 4 is built for exactly that, and two runs of it usually settles the pattern.

Unit 11 taught if for something always true: if you heat ice, it melts. This unit teaches if for one occasion: if it rains tomorrow, I will take the bus. A learner who mixes them is not confused about grammar, they are confused about the claim being made. The test that separates them is to say every time in front of the sentence. If it still makes sense, no will is needed. If it sounds odd, the sentence is about one occasion and takes will.

The words for faults, refunds, guarantees and insurance are here as language, not as advice. Every text says so on its own last line. If a learner asks what would really happen in their own case, the honest answer is that the rules differ from place to place and from contract to contract, and this unit cannot tell them. What it can give them is the sentence they need in order to ask.

Speaking 5 and Writing 2 both ask for five steps. Count three visible things rather than judging the style: five steps, a verb at the start of every step, and at least two time words joining them. A learner who writes a good paragraph instead of a list has not done the task, because a set of instructions has to be followable one line at a time by somebody who has never done it.

selfAssessment.statement: I can say what I will do if something happens tomorrow.
I can join two moments in writing with while, until and as soon as.
I can answer a question about my plans without putting will in the time part.
I can say whether something is happening now or arranged for later.
I can tell someone the steps to follow when a machine stops working.
I can write a short numbered list of steps that somebody else can follow.
I can read a notice and find the step I have to follow.
I can listen to a set of instructions and write the steps in order.

assignment.title: The plan, and what I will do if it goes wrong
assignment.instructions:
Make one recording and write one short plan. You may invent every detail.
Part 1. The recording, about one minute.
Say what is arranged for one day next week. Use am, is or are plus an -ing verb, with a time word in every sentence.
Say two things that could go wrong. Use if plus the present and will, once for each.
Say what you will do as soon as the first thing is finished.
Say how long you will wait, using until.
Say your backup, using unless.
Give three steps you would follow if the plan failed, each starting with a verb.
Play the recording back and count the six things in the list above.
If one is missing, record it again. Do not add it in your head.
Part 2. The written plan.
Write two paragraphs, four to five sentences each.
Paragraph one: what is arranged, and at what time.
Paragraph two: what could go wrong, and what you will do in each case.
Under the two paragraphs, write a numbered list of three steps for the worst case. Start every step with a verb.
Check one thing before you finish. Every sentence has one will at most, and no will sits in a half that starts with if, when, until or as soon as.
Then write one line that starts: This shows I can …
assignment.submissionType: An audio recording and a written plan
